decisions.location: Section 5 Conclusion and discussion (chunk 45); see also Section 2.1 Monetary incentives (chunks 14-16) and Reference 5 (chunk 52)
decisions.quote: In this study we first replicated the original experiment of Asch [ 1 – 3 ] with 5 confederates and ten line tasks. We find an average error rate of 33% which replicates the original findings of Asch very closely and which is in line with other replications that were conducted predominately with American students [ 12 ]. Together with recent studies from Japan [ 14 ], and Bosnia and Herzegowina [ 15 ], our study provides further evidence that the influence of groups on individuals’ judgments is a universal phenomenon, and is still valid today. Furthermore, we incentivized the decisions and find a drop of the error rate by 8%-points to 25%. Hence, monetary incentives do not eliminate the effect of group pressure. This finding sheds doubt on former results which predominately show the opposite effect, namely that incentives increase compliance [ 5 ,  6 ].
decisions.reason: Section 2.1 reviews Baron et al. [5] (1996) on monetary incentives in conformity (decreasing conformity by half to 15% on easy eyewitness tasks but increasing compliance on difficult tasks), notes its small sample size, and derives H2 (rewards for nonconformity decrease group pressure). Franzen and Mader (2023) empirically test randomized piece-rate monetary incentives (1 CHF per correct line judgment, n=103 vs n=99) across easy and hard critical trials (Fig 1), finding an 8%-point reduction in conformity to 25%, and explicitly contrast this outcome in Section 5 against [5, 6] as shedding doubt on former results showing that incentives increase compliance. Although the current study uses an Asch line task and does not re-estimate a formal reward-by-difficulty interaction term, this is a direct conceptual empirical retest and explicit results comparison against Baron et al.'s (1996) directional incentive claim. Baron et al. (1996) is absent from shipped row 6 (Asch, 1956) and sibling targets.

decisions.reason: Section 2.1 reviews Bhanot and Williamson [6] (2020), who found that trial-level monetary incentives ($0-$3) for correct answers increased majority alignment in online trivia experiments, and uses this conflicting evidence to motivate H2 (that rewards for nonconformity decrease group pressure). Franzen and Mader (2023) empirically test a randomized 1 CHF per correct answer incentive in the Asch task (Group 2 vs Group 1), finding that incentives reduce the error rate by 8 percentage points to 25% (1.97 to 1.47 errors, p=0.03), and explicitly conclude in Section 5 that their finding 'sheds doubt on former results which predominately show the opposite effect, namely that incentives increase compliance [ 5 ,  6 ].' Under the codebook, changing from online trivia herding to a laboratory Asch task does not exclude a conceptual replication when the published directional claim is empirically retested and explicitly compared. Bhanot and Williamson (2020) is absent from shipped row 6 (Asch, 1956) and sibling targets.

decisions.location: Section 5 Conclusion and discussion (chunk 45); see also Section 2.1 Monetary incentives (chunks 15-16) and Reference 7 (chunk 52)
decisions.quote: In this study we first replicated the original experiment of Asch [ 1 – 3 ] with 5 confederates and ten line tasks. We find an average error rate of 33% which replicates the original findings of Asch very closely and which is in line with other replications that were conducted predominately with American students [ 12 ]. Together with recent studies from Japan [ 14 ], and Bosnia and Herzegowina [ 15 ], our study provides further evidence that the influence of groups on individuals’ judgments is a universal phenomenon, and is still valid today. Furthermore, we incentivized the decisions and find a drop of the error rate by 8%-points to 25%. Hence, monetary incentives do not eliminate the effect of group pressure. This finding sheds doubt on former results which predominately show the opposite effect, namely that incentives increase compliance [ 5 ,  6 ].
decisions.reason: Section 2.1 reviews Fujita and Mori [7] (2017) as finding that 'the conformity effect disappears in the individually incentivized condition' of the Asch line task, criticizes its small sample size (only 10 subjects in the individualized minority incentive condition) and fMORI trick detection, and cites [7] in formulating H2. Franzen and Mader (2023) test individual piece-rate monetary rewards for accurate line judgments in a higher-powered confederate Asch design (n=103 incentivized vs n=99 non-incentivized), finding an 8%-point reduction to a 25% error rate, and explicitly conclude in Section 5: 'Hence, monetary incentives do not eliminate the effect of group pressure.' Even without repeating the collective-payoff arm, fMORI glasses, or repeating '[7]' in that Discussion sentence, the current study empirically retests and directly answers Fujita and Mori's specific published claim that individual incentives eliminate Asch conformity. Fujita and Mori (2017) is absent from shipped row 6 (Asch, 1956) and sibling targets.

corrected_value.title: A semantic mismatch effect on serial recall: Evidence for interlexical processing of irrelevant speech.

decisions.location: Discussion (chunk 38); see also Introduction (chunks 8-11), Results (chunks 21, 24), Discussion (chunk 35), and References (chunk 47)
decisions.reason: Röer and Cowan (2020/2021) review Röer, Bell, Körner, & Buchner (2019) in the Introduction (chunk 8) for the finding that semantically unexpected sentence-final words in irrelevant speech disrupt serial recall more than expected endings, and make testing whether semantically unexpected words are detected or disrupt shadowing in dichotic selective listening Purpose (1) of the study (chunk 11). They manipulate expected versus unexpected proverb endings within-subjects (N=80), find strong Bayesian evidence for the null on shadowing errors (BF10=0.060, chunk 24) and near-zero retrospective detection (1/80, chunk 21), and explicitly contrast their null findings with Röer et al. (2019) in the Discussion (chunks 35, 38), concluding that cross-modal distraction findings do not generalize to unimodal auditory selective listening. Primary abstract facts (0089) confirm Röer et al. (2019) reports 5 cross-modal serial-recall experiments establishing this semantic mismatch effect. Under the codebook, this cross-paradigm generalizability test is a conceptual replication absent from shipped row 144 (Moray, 1959).

Röer, Buchner, & Bell (in press) ('Auditory distraction in short-term memory: Stable effects of semantic mismatches on serial recall', Auditory Perception & Cognition 2(3), 143-162, print issue date 2019-07-03, online 2020-01-28, DOI 10.1080/25742442.2020.1722560) is co-cited once in the Introduction (chunk 8) alongside Röer et al. (2019) for the claim that semantically unexpected sentence endings disrupt serial recall more than expected endings, whereas the Discussion (chunk 35) cites only Röer et al. (2019). From the original-primary research context (0089), only metadata and a secondary indexed abstract were accessible for Röer, Buchner, & Bell (in press) (describing two experiments on nonhabituation/repetition of distractor sentences and citing Röer et al., 2019); its primary full text/methods were blocked (HTTP 403). Because the current study does not test habituation across repeated sentences and the primary report/cohort relationship between the 2019 and in-press papers remains unverified, whether target 5 is a distinct retested target cannot be determined.

decisions.location: Discussion (chunk 16); see also Results Tables 3-5 (chunks 10-13), Discussion (chunk 15), and Reference 14 (chunks 24-25)
decisions.quote: his study [14]. There have been several reports for the association between FTO and BMI [6–12], and two of them referred to rs8044769 as BMI associated SNP [11, 12]. So, we suspected that the association between rs8044769 and BMI may contribute to the association between this SNP and OA in the GWAS study. However, in our study, rs8044769 was not associated with BMI, and it might be another reason for the negative association between rs8044769 and OA.From our data we cannot get a conclusion that FTO is not associated with BMI in Chinese population as the allele and genotype differences of rs8044769 do not equal to changes of FTO function or FTO expression. Some other genetic variants in FTO might be associated with BMI or OA in Chinese population, and further studies are needed to evaluate the association of FTO with BMI and OA.The associations among rs8044769, BMI, and OA drew attentions to some concern on current GWAS results. Shortcomings like the imprecise phenotype definitions, chosen criterion, and limited study populations in the GWAS may lead to some false-positive association
decisions.reason: Verified primary source facts (0097) establish that Panoutsopoulou et al. (2014, Ref 14, PMC4251538) expanded the arcOGEN discovery sample across seven cohorts (increasing knee-OA cases by 55%, hip-OA cases by 57%, and controls by 69%) and reported a newly added, direct rs8044769-overweight/BMI association irrespective of OA status (10,538 overweight/obese vs 4,598 normal-weight subjects, G-allele OR=1.14, 95% CI 1.08-1.19, p=7.5e-7) as well as BMI-category-stratified OA analyses, separate from its instrumental-variable Mendelian randomisation mediation analysis and beyond the female BMI-adjusted OA attenuation already in Zeggini et al. (2012, Ref 13, shipped row 1152). Dai et al. (2018) directly test this added rs8044769-overweight/obese and quantitative BMI association component in 890 knee-OA cases and 844 controls (Tables 4-5) plus BMI-stratified OA (Table 3), and explicitly contrast their null SNP-BMI result against Ref 14 in Discussion (chunks 15-16). Thus Ref 14 contributes a distinct empirically retested finding absent from shipped row 1152.
